sentences.text: Dimorphodon exhibited primitive characteristics, including a very small braincase and proportionally short wings.
Adult Dimorphodon measured about 1 meter in body length with a wingspan of 1.45 meters.
Dimorphodon had a long tail composed of thirty vertebrae.
Dimorphodon had a large, bulky skull about 23 cm long that was lightened by large openings separated by thin bony partitions.
Dimorphodon had proportionally short wings and a robust skeleton that offered very little gliding potential.
Dimorphodon had an elongated, clawless fifth toe that was oriented to the side.
Dimorphodon had a large, voluminous skull whose weight was reduced by large cavities separated by thin bony walls.
Dimorphodon had a strong and flexible beak that may have possessed a lower membranous pouch.
The holotype specimen of Dimorphodon, NHMUK PV R1034, is a partial and disarticulated skeleton that lacks a skull.
The species name macronyx refers to the large claws on the hand of the animal.
The well-preserved foot of D. weintraubi shows that pterosaurs had a plantigrade gait rather than a digitigrade posture.
The first fossils attributed to Dimorphodon were discovered by Mary Anning at Lyme Regis, Dorset, in December 1828.
The genus Dimorphodon was named by Richard Owen in 1859.
Richard Owen found two new specimens of Dimorphodon in 1858 that included skulls, which were previously missing from earlier finds.
Recent studies suggest Dimorphodon likely hunted small vertebrates while also consuming small invertebrates like insects.
Dental microwear examinations confirm Dimorphodon was a vertebrate predator, though it may have occasionally eaten softer invertebrates.
Dimorphodon was a competent climber with proportionally large and curved claws.
Like modern squirrels, Dimorphodon probably moved in a saltatorial (leaping) manner while climbing.
Research suggests that Dimorphodon's poor flying ability was a developed trait rather than an ancestral characteristic.
Dimorphodon macronyx, described by Buckland in 1829, is the type species of the genus.
In 1870, Seeley assigned Dimorphodon to its own family, Dimorphodontidae.
Dimorphodon lived in Europe during the Early Jurassic Period, approximately 201 to 191 million years ago.
Fossil remains of Dimorphodon have been found in England.
Dimorphodon probably lived in coastal regions.
Researchers have debated whether Dimorphodon was primarily an insectivore or a piscivore.
Mark Witton argues that Dimorphodon was a specialized carnivore too large for an insectivorous diet, likely hunting small vertebrates despite its relatively weak jaw musculature.
Richard Owen speculated that Dimorphodon was a quadruped with a membrane between the tail and legs, making it ungainly on the ground.
